key_terms.meaning: The number of independent quantities a device can report or the user can control; a position in 3D plus an orientation needs 6, so a full tracker is 6-DOF.
Ratio of movement shown on the display to movement made on the input device; gain above 1 makes small hand moves cover large virtual distances.
The pair (position, orientation) of an object in a fixed frame, written as a translation vector plus a rotation.
Delay between a real movement and the system's response, measured in milliseconds; it adds a false lag the user feels as swimming or lag.
The volume of space in which a tracker can report a valid pose, given in metres or cubic metres.
Slow growth of pose error over time, typical of trackers that integrate rate signals instead of measuring absolute position.
A tracker that fuses two or more families (for example inertial plus optical) so one supplies fast rates and the other supplies absolute correction.
A navigation method that changes the viewpoint's position in the virtual world, such as teleport, fly, or walk-in-place.
A manipulation method where the virtual arm grows non-linearly beyond the physical reach, letting the user touch distant objects with natural hand motion.
A glove fitted with bend sensors and often a tracker, so the system reads finger angles and hand pose directly.
A strip whose electrical resistance rises as it bends; glued over a knuckle it converts finger angle into a voltage.
A static gesture is a held hand shape (open palm, fist); a dynamic gesture is a hand path in time (a swipe or a circle).
Recording the joint motion of a real performer and replaying it as a moving skeleton, so animation follows real body mechanics.
Solving for joint angles that place an end point (hand, foot) at a measured position, using the skeleton's bone lengths as constraints.
A chipset holding accelerometers and gyroscopes, often a magnetometer, that reports linear acceleration and angular rate.
A sensor that measures distance from the travel time of a light pulse: d = c·t/2, with c the speed of light and t the round-trip time.
Combining readings from several sensors, usually with a Kalman or complementary filter, to get a better estimate than any one sensor gives.
The three head angles: yaw turns left-right about the vertical axis, pitch nods up-down, roll tilts ear to shoulder.
The direction of gravity measured by an accelerometer at rest; it gives an absolute reference for pitch and roll.
A base station sweeps laser or LED beams across the room while headset sensors time each hit, so angles and then position are computed without a camera on the headset.

takeaways: An input device is a channel with limited degrees of freedom, a mapping to the task, and a feedback path; the same task can feel easy or impossible depending on that mapping.
Desktop devices such as the mouse and joystick are the reference point: they are precise and cheap but were never designed for 3D rotation.
Every tracker family sits somewhere on a trade-off between workspace, accuracy, latency, update rate and immunity to interference, so no single tracker is best.
Position tracking alone is not interaction: navigation, selection and manipulation techniques are the layer that turns pose data into usable action.
Techniques are chosen to match distance and precision, so teleport suits a large world while direct hand reach suits an arm's-length task.
A data glove measures hand shape; a gesture interface adds recognition, and the hard part is separating intended gestures from ordinary hand movement.
Body and hand tracking reconstruct a skeleton from noisy sensors, and motion capture is the same reconstruction used to drive animation.
Every sensor measures one physical quantity and carries its own noise, bias and drift, which is why practical systems fuse several sensors.
A headset gets yaw from the gyroscope and pitch and roll from gravity, then removes slow gyroscope drift with an external reference such as lighthouse beams.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are usually comparison-plus-application: a table of tracker or input-device characteristics followed by a justified choice for a stated VR or AR task.

bank.q: Define pose and explain why a 3D position tracker must report six numbers rather than three.
outline: Pose = position vector plus orientation; six values in a fixed frame
Three translations alone cannot fix where the head or hand is looking
3-DOF orientation-only trackers and why they are insufficient for reaching tasks
Example: looking around versus picking up a virtual object

bank.q: List the characteristics by which an input device is judged and explain each in one or two lines.
outline: Degrees of freedom, resolution and accuracy
Control-display gain and mapping to the task
Latency and update rate
Feedback: visual, audio, haptic
Physical comfort, fatigue, learning time, cost

bank.q: Describe the four main families of 3D position trackers, giving the physical principle and one strong and one weak point of each.
outline: Mechanical: linked arms and encoders; accurate, small workspace
Magnetic: transmitter coils and sensor coils; no line of sight, metal and field distortion
Optical: cameras or LEDs and markers; large workspace, occlusion and lighting
Inertial: accelerometers and gyroscopes; fast and inside-out, drift over time

bank.q: Explain how a data glove measures finger bend and how the readings are turned into a hand pose.
outline: Flex or bend sensors at the knuckles change resistance with curvature
Voltage divider and ADC per finger; calibration at flat and fully bent
Hand pose from finger angles plus a wrist or glove tracker
Limitations: no force sensing, cross-talk, glove fit differs per user

bank.q: Explain how yaw, pitch and roll of the head are obtained from a gyroscope and an accelerometer, and why the two are combined.
outline: Gyroscope gives angular rate; integrate once for angle
Integration accumulates drift and bias
Accelerometer gives the gravity vector at rest, so absolute pitch and roll
Yaw has no gravity reference and needs a magnetometer or external beacon
Complementary or Kalman filter combines high-rate and absolute data

bank.q: A user must pick a small component on a distant shelf in a large virtual factory. Choose a navigation technique and a manipulation technique, and justify both.
outline: Large distance favours teleport or scaled fly over real walking
Precision at distance favours ray casting or go-go extended reach
Gain and confirmation feedback to avoid mis-selection
Why direct hand reach fails beyond arm's length
Combine: teleport close, then direct manipulation

bank.q: A tracker updates at 120 Hz and the pipeline adds 25 ms of latency. A hand moves at 1.2 m/s. Compute the positional error in the display and state whether the error is acceptable for touching a virtual button 4 cm wide.
outline: Lag distance = speed × latency = 1.2 × 0.025 = 0.03 m = 3 cm
Update period = 1/120 s ≈ 8.3 ms
Compare 3 cm with target size 4 cm: marginal, so prediction or higher rate needed
Distinguish latency from update rate

bank.q: You must build a low-cost hand gesture input for a phone-based AR app. Select the sensors and the recognition approach, and defend the choice against a data glove.
outline: Camera plus computer vision, markerless hand skeleton from landmarks
Depth or ToF sensor to segment the hand from the background
Static shapes by classifier, dynamic gestures by template or sequence model
Glove gives accurate angles but needs hardware and fitting
Lighting, occluded fingers, battery and processing limits on a phone

bank.q: A magnetic tracker is to be installed in a room with steel furniture and CRT monitors. Analyse the expected errors and propose a remedy using tracker selection or hybrid design.
outline: Ferromagnetic metal and electric currents distort the field
Errors appear as jitter and wrong position, not clean noise
Options: move the workspace, shield, calibrate, or switch to optical or inertial
Hybrid: inertial rates corrected by optical fixes
State the trade-off honestly: no zero-cost fix

bank.q: Compare mechanical, magnetic, optical and inertial trackers on workspace, accuracy, latency, update rate and immunity to interference, and recommend one for a seated head-mounted VR setup and one for a room-scale multi-user setup.
outline: Structured table across the five criteria
Mechanical: high accuracy, tiny workspace, heavy
Magnetic: no occlusion, distortion-prone
Optical outside-in: large workspace, occlusion and cost
Inertial: cheap and fast, drifting alone, good when fused
Justified recommendation with a stated assumption

bank.q: Drift is unavoidable in inertial head tracking. Explain its origin, and evaluate the lighthouse approach as a way of removing it.
outline: Bias in gyroscope output integrates into angle error that grows with time
Gravity fixes pitch and roll but not yaw
Lighthouse base station sweeps beams; sensors time the hits
Angles from timing, then position by triangulation; periodic absolute fix resets drift
Costs: base station setup, line of sight to the emitters, room calibration

bank.q: Analyse how a motion capture pipeline turns recorded sensor data into an animated skeleton, and identify where error enters at each stage.
outline: Sensors: markers, inertial suits, or camera images
Correspondence and labelling of markers to joints
Noise and occlusion causing gaps; interpolation
Fitting: bone lengths fixed, joint angles solved by IK; ambiguity of rotation
Retargeting to a different character changes proportions and foot contact
Filtering and cleanup as the practical fix

bank.q: Gesture interfaces remove the button but add fatigue and ambiguity. Evaluate gesture input against a handheld controller for a public self-service kiosk, using arm fatigue, hygiene, lighting and user diversity as criteria.
outline: Gorilla arm from unsupported mid-air pointing
Hygiene argument: no shared touch surface
Lighting and background affect camera-based recognition
User diversity: hand size, skin tone, sleeve, disability
Ambiguity and false triggers; need for dwell or confirmation feedback
Recommendation with a mixed design: gestures for coarse choice, one physical control for confirm

bank.q: A wrist-worn inertial unit drives hand tracking for AR. Evaluate which sensors it needs, how fusion is done, and where the design will fail in practice.
outline: Accelerometer for gravity, gyroscope for rate, magnetometer for heading
Complementary or Kalman filter; quaternion orientation output
Position cannot come from a wrist IMU alone without a model
Failures: magnetic disturbance indoors, drift in yaw, no absolute position, gesture ambiguity
Practical fix: occasional camera-based correction

glossary.def: Any hardware that carries the user's intention, position or body state into the computing system.
An input whose displacement changes with the force or motion applied, such as a joystick or mouse, so position is sensed rather than force.
An input that senses force while barely moving, such as a force-sensing stick, so the user gets no travel feedback from the device.
A six-degree-of-freedom desktop controller, often a sprung puck, used to rotate and move a model in CAD work.
How close the reported value is to the true value, in the same units, stated as an error or a percentage of range.
The smallest change in the measured quantity that the device can report.
Small random frame-to-frame variation in the reported pose while the object is actually still.
How many pose samples the tracker delivers per second, in hertz.
The coordinate system, with an origin and axes, in which a pose is expressed.
Tracking where sensors fixed in the room observe markers on the user.
Tracking where cameras or sensors on the headset or device observe the room.
Estimating the current pose by adding up integrated motion since the last known absolute fix.
A navigation technique that jumps the viewpoint to a marked point, removing the motion that causes simulator sickness.
Selection by pointing a virtual ray from the hand or head and choosing the first object it meets, good for distant targets.
A selection technique where a ray picks the object and the hand then grabs it at a scaled arm length.
Muscle fatigue from holding the arm raised in mid-air for long periods, the main cost of gesture interfaces.
A sensor whose resistance or capacitance changes with curvature, used along the fingers of a data glove.
Bringing thumb and index finger together, the most common grab gesture in hand-tracked interfaces.
Motion capture that tracks reflective or active markers attached to the body and solves their positions from camera images.
Motion capture that finds body or hand joints directly in camera images without physical markers.
A sensor that measures proper acceleration, which at rest is the gravity vector and during motion is gravity plus movement.
A sensor that measures angular rate; its output is integrated over time to give angle.
A sensor that measures the local magnetic field direction, giving an absolute heading reference for yaw.
A constant offset in a sensor's output that is present even when the true input is zero.
A depth-sensing method that projects a known pattern and solves the shape from how the pattern deforms.
A fixed emitter that broadcasts reference signals, such as lighthouse sweeps, for other devices to measure against.
